title: Entrepreneurship
tagline: What makes an entrepreneur, the types Danhof identified, the five phases of starting up, and how business risk is managed.

overview.intro: An entrepreneur is not merely someone who owns a business. The distinguishing act is the bearing of risk in pursuit of an opportunity, organising the resources needed to exploit it, and accepting the uncertainty of the outcome. This unit covers the meaning and qualities of entrepreneurship, Danhof’s classification of entrepreneurs, the related idea of intrapreneurship inside a large organisation, the practical sequence of setting up an enterprise through its five business phases, and business risk: its causes, the signs of failure and the methods by which a firm manages risk to stay alive.

facts.label: Danhof’s types
facts.value: Innovating entrepreneur, adaptive entrepreneur, primitive or garibi entrepreneur, and third category of government entrepreneurs.

facts.label: Five phases
facts.value: Establishment, growth, maturity, expansion and decline, each with its own demands on the founder.

facts.label: Risk classes
facts.value: Business risk from operations, financial risk from borrowing, market risk from demand, and human risk from people.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Qualities of an entrepreneur, the phases and risk management are the regular theory questions in this unit.

learningOutcomes: Define entrepreneurship and state the qualities an entrepreneur needs.
Explain Danhof’s types of entrepreneurs with examples.
Describe intrapreneurship and how it differs from entrepreneurship.
Outline the five phases of setting up and running an enterprise.
Classify business risks and explain methods of managing them.

learn.title: The entrepreneur, entrepreneurship and the qualities required

blocks.text: Entrepreneurship is the process of designing, launching and running a new business, initially a small one, bearing its risks in the hope of profit and growth. The entrepreneur is the person who performs this function: she spots an opportunity that others have not acted on, commits her own resources and often those of others, organises men, money and materials, and accepts the possibility of loss as the price of the chance of gain. Joseph Schumpeter described the entrepreneur as the agent of creative destruction, the person whose new combination makes existing methods obsolete.

items: Innovation: offering a new product, process, market or source of supply.
Risk bearing: accepting the uncertainty that other people avoid.
Vision and foresight: seeing where demand will be rather than where it is.
Decisiveness: choosing under incomplete information and living with the choice.
Persistence: continuing through the early years of weak cash flow.
Leadership and people skill: attracting and holding capable people without a famous brand.
Self-confidence coupled with realism about what has gone wrong.

blocks.caption: Qualities of an entrepreneur and what each delivers
rows: Creates a product or method competitors cannot yet match
Makes the venture possible where a salaried person would not attempt it
Places the firm where demand will be, not where it was
Keeps the organisation moving when growth slows
Turns an idea into a working operation with limited resources

items.text: A designer starts a brand using recycled fabric after noticing a shift in consumer taste.
items.note: The opportunity existed for everyone; only the entrepreneur acted on it and accepted the risk.

items.text: A first-generation founder invests savings in a cold-chain vehicle without a guaranteed contract.
items.note: Risk bearing with own resources is the defining commitment rather than a salaried role.

learn.title: Danhof’s types of entrepreneurs and intrapreneurship

blocks.text: Clifford Danhof classified entrepreneurs into three broad groups, to which a fourth was later added. The innovating entrepreneur introduces a new good or a new method of production, opens a new market, or finds a new source of supply. The adaptive entrepreneur adopts established methods with modification, adjusting the business to current conditions rather than creating them, and is typical of small traders. The primitive or garibi entrepreneur works with traditional methods, small capital and modest ambition, operating in the unorganised sector. The government entrepreneur runs an enterprise created and financed by the state.

blocks.caption: Danhof’s classification of entrepreneurs
rows: Introduces new goods, methods, markets or supplies
Traditional methods, small capital, limited growth aim
Enterprise set up and run by the state

blocks.text: Intrapreneurship is entrepreneurship practised inside an existing organisation. An intrapreneur develops a new product, service or process using the resources and within the authority of the employer, but carries the risk and the credit differently: the organisation bears the financial risk while the individual carries the professional risk of failure. Intrapreneurship gives large firms the freshness of a startup without the overhead, and gives individuals a route to test ideas without leaving a salary.

items: The entrepreneur bears financial and personal risk; the intrapreneur bears mainly career risk.
The entrepreneur raises capital externally; the intrapreneur competes for internal budget.
The entrepreneur builds the organisation; the intrapreneur works within one.
Both share the same core activity: recognising an opportunity and organising resources to exploit it.

learn.title: Setting up an enterprise: the five business phases

blocks.text: A new enterprise passes through identifiable phases, and each demands a different skill from the founder. In the establishment phase the idea is tested, the legal form chosen, finance arranged and the first customers won; the work is hands-on and cash is scarce. In the growth phase sales rise, staff are added, systems begin to replace personal supervision, and the founder must start delegating. In the maturity phase the business is stable, processes are documented, and the challenge is efficiency and defending market share.

blocks.caption: The five phases and the founder’s central task
rows: Idea tested, entity formed, first sales made
New products, markets or branches added
Sales fall as conditions or competition change
Decide to renew, reposition or exit

blocks.text: Expansion is the phase where firms fail most unexpectedly, because growth consumes cash faster than profit can supply it. Decline is not inevitable: many firms renew themselves by innovating into the next cycle, while others manage a deliberate and orderly exit.

items.text: A bakery that outgrows its kitchen and takes a second unit with a bank loan.
items.note: The expansion phase has been entered, and finance must be arranged before the capacity is needed.

items.text: A founder who still approves every purchase after hiring a professional manager.
items.note: The delegation step of the growth phase has been skipped, which slows the firm and frustrates the manager.

learn.title: Business risks, causes of failure and their management

blocks.text: Business risk is the possibility that the outcome of a decision will fall short of expectation, most sharply the possibility of loss. It arises from several causes: uncertainty of demand, the cost of production turning out higher than planned, competition forcing prices down, technological change making a product obsolete, poor management of working capital, and legal or political change. Failure rarely has a single cause; it usually combines an external shock with an internal weakness such as undercapitalisation or overtrading.

blocks.caption: Causes of business failure and the warning signs
rows: Cash balance falls every month regardless of sales
Sales rise while the bank overdraft rises faster
Debtors outstanding for long while creditors press for payment
Market share slips as a newer rival’s product gains attention
Decisions delayed, responsibilities unclear, staff turnover high
Notices, penalties and disputed licences accumulate

items: Diversify products and markets so that one failure does not sink the firm.
Match the term of finance to the term of the asset: never fund a fixed asset with a short loan.
Hold a cash reserve or a committed credit line for the lean season.
Insure against insurable risks such as fire, theft and transit loss.
Take advances and stage payments so that the buyer funds the working capital.
Use contractual protection: clear terms, written agreements and penalty clauses.
Review the plan against actual results frequently, and act on the variance early.

items.text: A textile trader funds looms with a twelve-month loan repaid from the first quarter’s profit.
items.note: The maturity mismatch between asset and finance is the classic route to a liquidity crisis.

items.text: A firm insures its warehouse stock against fire and simultaneously sprinkles the building.
items.note: Insurance transfers the financial impact while the sprinkler reduces the probability, showing two different risk tools together.

keyPoints: Entrepreneurship is designing, launching and running a new business while bearing its risks.
The entrepreneur’s defining acts are innovation, risk bearing and the organisation of resources.
Danhof classified entrepreneurs as innovating, adaptive, primitive or garibi, and government.
An adaptive entrepreneur modifies established methods instead of creating new ones.
An intrapreneur innovates inside an existing organisation and bears mainly career risk.
The five phases are establishment, growth, maturity, expansion and decline.
Growth and expansion phases consume cash faster than profit, which is when firms most often fail.
Causes of failure include undercapitalisation, overtrading, weak management and obsolete products.
Risk can be avoided, reduced, transferred by insurance, or accepted with a reserve.
Finance must be matched in term to the asset it funds.
examFocus: Qualities questions want the quality and what it achieves, not a bare list of adjectives.
In Danhof questions, give one example per type; the classification alone rarely earns full marks.
Risk-management answers should pair each method with the specific risk it treats, which is what examiners use to separate strong from weak scripts.

vocabulary.meaning: Person who designs, launches and runs a business, bearing its risks for potential gain.
Process of creating and running an enterprise under conditions of risk and uncertainty.
Employee who develops new products or processes using the resources of an existing organisation.
Grouping of entrepreneurs as innovating, adaptive, primitive or government.
Possibility of a loss or an outcome below expectation in the running of a business.
Condition in which the capital of a firm is too small for the operations it attempts.
Rising sales financed by short-term borrowing faster than cash is collected.

questions.prompt: The quality that most distinguishes an entrepreneur from a salaried manager is:
questions.explanation: The entrepreneur commits her own resources and accepts the possibility of loss, which the salaried manager does not.

questions.prompt: An entrepreneur who adopts established methods with modifications to suit current conditions is classified by Danhof as:
questions.explanation: The adaptive entrepreneur works with proven methods and adapts them rather than creating anything new.

questions.prompt: An intrapreneur differs from an entrepreneur mainly in that:
options: The intrapreneur takes no risk of any kind
The organisation bears the financial risk while the individual bears career risk
The intrapreneur has no access to resources
Intrapreneurship applies only to government bodies
questions.answer: The organisation bears the financial risk while the individual bears career risk
questions.explanation: Both innovate, but the funding and the consequence of failure differ: the employer finances the idea and the employee’s reputation carries the downside.

questions.prompt: A firm with rising sales and a faster-rising bank overdraft is showing the classic sign of:
questions.explanation: Sales financed by short-term borrowing faster than cash is collected is overtrading, and the rising overdraft is its visible signature.

questions.prompt: The five phases of an enterprise are establishment, growth, maturity, expansion and __________ .
questions.explanation: The final phase is decline, which the firm can answer with renewal and innovation or manage as an orderly exit.

questions.prompt: The technique of transferring the financial impact of an insurable risk to an insurer is called __________ .
questions.explanation: Insurance does not reduce the chance of the event; it shifts the money consequence to another party in return for a premium.

questions.prompt: State any four qualities required of a successful entrepreneur.
questions.answer: Four qualities are innovation, which produces something the market does not yet have; risk bearing, which means accepting the possibility of loss; foresight, which places the firm where demand will be; and organising ability, which converts an idea into a working operation with limited resources. Persistence and leadership are also expected.
questions.explanation: Each quality needs a line showing what it contributes, because a bare list earns only partial credit.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between an entrepreneur and an intrapreneur.
questions.answer: An entrepreneur starts and runs her own venture, raising capital externally and bearing both the financial and the personal risk of failure. An innovating employee inside an existing organisation, by contrast, is an intrapreneur: the employer provides the capital and the infrastructure, while the individual carries mainly the professional or career risk. Both perform the same core function of recognising an opportunity and organising resources to exploit it.
questions.explanation: The comparison must cover risk and control of capital, and then note the shared core activity.

questions.prompt: Explain the five phases of a business with the central task of the founder in each.
questions.answer: The establishment phase covers registration, finance and the first customers, where the founder’s task is to prove demand while conserving cash. In the growth phase sales and headcount rise, and the founder must build systems and begin delegating rather than supervising personally. The maturity phase brings stability and documented processes, where the task shifts to efficiency and defending market share. In the expansion phase the firm adds products, markets or branches, and the founder must fund that growth without losing control of the business. Finally, the decline phase shows falling sales, where the founder must decide between renewing through innovation, repositioning, or a managed exit.
questions.explanation: Each phase needs its own description and its own founder task; describing the phases without the tasks earns only about half marks.

questions.prompt: A young entrepreneur has launched a food delivery service, is funding delivery vehicles with a four-year bank loan repaid monthly, holds no cash reserve, and has seen a rival launch a cheaper app-based service. Identify the risks, classify them, and recommend how each should be managed.
questions.answer: The first risk is financial: a four-year asset is being repaid on a monthly schedule from operating cash, so any seasonal dip in orders creates a default risk. It should be managed by matching the term, taking the loan over the vehicle’s life with a grace period, or by leasing instead. The second is market risk: the rival’s cheaper app threatens demand. It should be managed by differentiation on delivery time, packaging and service rather than competing on price alone, and by reviewing costs. The third is liquidity risk arising from having no cash reserve, which should be addressed by building a reserve equal to two months of fixed costs and arranging a committed overdraft. The fourth is human risk, since the service depends on a small team of riders, and can be managed with contracts, incentive pay and a trained reserve of part-time riders.
questions.explanation: Marks depend on separating financial, market, liquidity and human risk and then matching a specific treatment to each, rather than listing generic advice.
